constraints: Representative investigations can be evaluated by the research team.
Cost optimization will follow only after the task-quality floor is established.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For a high-volume routine task with tight operating budgets, an efficient candidate may be the appropriate first benchmark; this pilot has different priorities.
details.errorCorrection: A weak starting model can create a false negative about feasibility, while general benchmarks and component-level accuracy do not establish the quality of the complete investigation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a capability-first starting point for complex reasoning and accuracy-sensitive work, followed by evaluation and efficiency optimization.
details.scenarioApplication: Evaluate representative investigations with the strongest suitable configuration, inspect the quality boundary, and compare lower-cost configurations only against that established standard.
details.transfer: Choose the initial evaluation baseline according to the uncertainty being resolved: capability feasibility or operating efficiency.

messages.text: Failure of the cheapest model does not establish that the task is infeasible with suitable capability.
Fixing the tier from unrelated benchmarks precedes the task-specific evidence that the team needs.
Accurate components can still produce an inadequate synthesis; component-level scores do not establish the end-to-end research quality.

feedback.reason: The initial decision is whether the research task can meet its quality requirement. A capability-first baseline separates feasibility from later cost reduction.

options.text: Begin with the strongest suitable capability on real investigations, establish the quality floor, and then test where cheaper configurations preserve it.
Begin with the cheapest model on every subtask and interpret its initial failures as evidence about whether the overall research workflow is feasible.
Choose a mid-tier model from general reasoning benchmarks and fix that tier before the team designs its investigation evaluation.
Decompose investigations into calls to efficient models and use component-level accuracy as the feasibility signal before evaluating the complete synthesis.

prompt: A scientific team is testing whether Claude can support nuanced investigations that take several hours. The initial study has few cases and prioritizes reasoning quality over interactive latency or per-call price. Which starting baseline best tests feasibility?

constraints: The failing exception slice is identifiable.
Candidate models can run on the actual prompt and evidence with latency and cost measurement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If all models fail on the same missing evidence, repair the request or retrieval rather than interpreting the result as a reason to buy more model capability.
details.errorCorrection: A global upgrade or repeated sampling assumes a solution without diagnosing the slice. Prompt changes judged only by the aggregate can leave the rare failure hidden.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends benchmark tests using actual prompts and data, then comparing accuracy, quality, edge cases, and cost.
details.scenarioApplication: Build the labeled exception benchmark, hold the request shape stable, and compare quality, latency, and cost across candidates while checking ordinary-case regressions.
details.transfer: Use the distribution of consequential errors, not just average accuracy, to decide where additional capability is warranted.

messages.text: The change may cost more without fixing the specific exception, and the aggregate report can conceal the same failure again.
Repeated agreement does not prove exception correctness and adds cost to all requests without evidence that sampling variance is the cause.
Examples may help, but the proposed aggregate-only acceptance test cannot establish whether the jurisdictional exception improved.

feedback.reason: An acceptable aggregate can conceal a capability gap on rare cases. Slice-level comparison is needed before deciding whether the model, routing, or another part of the request should change.

options.text: Upgrade all traffic to the strongest model and judge the change from the next aggregate accuracy report.
Add a second pass using the current model for every request, accepting exceptions when both passes agree.
Compare candidates on the exception and ordinary slices, then choose a capability change, targeted route, or human path supported by the results.
Add jurisdiction examples to the production prompt and retain the current model if its overall quality and cost remain within their previous ranges.

prompt: A compliance classifier selected mainly for price meets average accuracy, but misses rare jurisdictional exceptions. Those exceptions can be labeled and replayed. What should guide the next model decision?

constraints: Image support must be verified for the target deployment.
Paired cases measure handwritten-field accuracy, latency, and cost for both paths.
Unsupported fields can be rejected or sent to a person.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If direct images did not improve the required fields enough to justify their cost or latency, keep the evaluated OCR path with explicit handling for omitted fields.
details.errorCorrection: Better instructions cannot recover pixels absent from the text, API acceptance does not prove extraction accuracy, and fluent answers do not establish correct totals.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Claude accepts image content blocks for visual analysis. Choosing direct images over an OCR-only pipeline here depends on the stated paired workload measurements, not a guaranteed accuracy advantage.
details.scenarioApplication: Replay the same representative forms through OCR-text and supported image requests, compare the handwritten slice, and retain a manual or rejected-field path where neither is reliable.
details.transfer: Evaluate the evidence available to the model as well as the model itself when comparing input capabilities.

messages.text: A strong score on other text fields cannot establish accuracy for handwriting that OCR omitted from the request.
Confirmed image support and an operating-cost comparison still do not show the paired field-accuracy benefit required to set the production default.
Preserving recognized characters cannot restore omitted handwriting, and answer fluency is not the missing-field accuracy metric.

feedback.reason: The text pipeline has already discarded relevant evidence. Direct image support makes another input path possible, but its suitability still depends on the actual field benchmark and operating constraints.

options.text: Retain OCR because the text-only evaluation score is high, and use stronger extraction instructions for the missing handwritten totals.
Route all forms to direct images after image support is confirmed, and compare operating cost before setting the production default.
Increase OCR text resolution in the prompt by preserving every recognized character and compare average answer fluency across the two paths.
Verify image support and compare paired field accuracy and operating costs; choose direct images only when their measured benefit meets the deployment gates.

prompt: An invoice pipeline sends OCR text to Claude. On damaged forms the OCR omits handwritten totals, although they remain visible in the photographs. The team can test direct image input to the target model. What should determine the input-path choice?

constraints: The patch format is a required machine-consumed contract.
The quoted rates are measured scenario results, not provider guarantees.
Test-pass rates are measured among valid patches; rejected or unparseable patches cannot count as successful output.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If an evaluated repair or retry path brought S above the valid-patch floor within the latency and cost budgets, that complete path could be compared with R.
details.errorCorrection: Repair, routing mixtures, and retries might become evaluated designs, but their effectiveness and latency are not demonstrated by the single-attempt results given.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends testing with actual prompts and data and weighing performance and cost tradeoffs against use-case benchmarks.
details.scenarioApplication: Choose the candidate that meets the measured structural and task-quality requirements, then evaluate cost improvements against those same floors.
details.transfer: Select against the full production output contract rather than a general model score or one favorable outcome metric.

messages.text: The proposed repair layer is unvalidated; the provided results do not show that it restores the required patch contract.
A similar review score does not erase the measured difference in valid patches, and mixing in S does not demonstrate compliance with the floor.
Eventual retry success is a different system contract whose quality, latency, and cost must be measured rather than assumed.

feedback.reason: R satisfies both stated admission floors. S fails the required valid-patch contract; a cheaper price or higher score on another dimension cannot offset that hard boundary.

options.text: Select S because its higher test-pass rate measures the substantive code task, then repair malformed patch envelopes in downstream processing.
Select R for the current contract, verify its operating cost, and optimize only while preserving both production floors.
Alternate R and S to reduce average cost, using the shared code-review score as evidence that their patch contracts are equivalent.
Select S and request a second attempt for malformed patches, treating the original valid-patch floor as satisfied by eventual success.

prompt: Two code models have similar review scores. On representative repositories, R produces 99.5% valid patches and 96% test-passing patches; S produces 94% valid patches and 97% test-passing patches. Production requires at least 99% valid patches and 95% passing tests. Both meet the latency budget, but S is cheaper. Which selection is defensible?

constraints: The same held-out exception rubric gives the efficient model 88% and the stronger model 97%.
The legal quality floor is 95% and the service allows the stronger model's 2.8-second p95.
The exception workload is consequence-bearing, relatively small, and has a reviewer path.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the efficient model reached 95% on the exception slice at 1.0 second, retain it and optimize cost before considering a stronger model.
details.errorCorrection: Waiting for complaints ignores the held-out evidence and exposes legal decisions to a known quality failure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a capability-first starting point for complex reasoning and accuracy-sensitive work, followed by evaluation and efficiency optimization. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Capability and quality are the gating criteria for this workload, so the efficient-first default must reverse when it fails the hard exception floor.
details.scenarioApplication: Start with the stronger suitable model for the exception workflow, validate it on representative cases, then test a lower-cost route only where quality remains above 95%.
details.transfer: Use measured slice quality, service limits, and authority boundaries together; choose the least complex route that clears every stated floor and revisit it when the evidence changes.

messages.text: Waiting for complaints ignores the held-out evidence and exposes legal decisions to a known quality failure.
The stronger model is appropriate for the exception floor, but capability-first does not remove the need to test a lower-cost route where the measured floor remains satisfied.
Average traffic can hide the consequence-bearing exception failure; the stated 95% floor must be evaluated on that representative slice.

feedback.reason: The stronger model is feasible within the stated latency and satisfies the consequence-bearing floor that the efficient model misses.

options.text: Start with the efficient model for all cases and upgrade only after broad production complaints appear.
Use the stronger model for every case and defer any efficiency experiment until the service has operated for a full release cycle.
Choose the model from average traffic accuracy and unit cost, without evaluating the rare exception slice separately.
Start capability-first with the stronger model, then test a lower-cost route only after it clears the quality floor.

prompt:
A tax-law assistant drafts positions for rare jurisdictional exceptions. The efficient model is 1.0 second p95 and $0.03 per case but reaches 88% on the exception rubric; the stronger model is 2.8 seconds and $0.12 but reaches 97%. The service allows 4 seconds and the legal quality floor is 95%.

Which model-selection sequence should govern this exception workflow?

constraints: Both models were measured on the same routine and high-risk classes; high-risk accuracy must be at least 98%.
The service p95 limit is 1.2 seconds and Model B may serve at most 20% of traffic.
The routed replay, including detector misses, reaches 98.8% high-risk accuracy at 1.1 seconds p95 with 18% Model B usage.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If end-to-end high-risk accuracy including detector misses fell below 98%, or mixed-route p95 exceeded 1.2 seconds, hold the affected rollout and redesign the route instead of inferring readiness from model-only scores.
details.errorCorrection: The global stronger route breaches p95 and budget, while the global efficient route fails the high-risk floor; the measured mixed route includes unrecognized false negatives in its end-to-end quality result and clears the stated floor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes multi-model strategies that use a lower-cost executor for most work and escalate difficult decisions to a stronger advisor or model. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The measured routed system, including false negatives, clears the high-risk quality floor, latency limit, and Model B allocation. Detector precision or model-only accuracy alone would not establish this.
details.scenarioApplication: Use Model A for routine requests and Model B for the detected high-risk slice, retain the separately flagged uncertainty review path, and monitor end-to-end high-risk accuracy including detector misses, routing volume, and 1.2-second p95 under production concurrency.
details.transfer: Use measured slice quality, service limits, and authority boundaries together; choose the least complex route that clears every stated floor and revisit it when the evidence changes.

messages.text: The global stronger route reaches 1.9 seconds p95 and exceeds both the 1.2-second service limit and the 20% allocation boundary.
Model A scores 93% on the high-risk class, below the 98% floor; low latency cannot justify the known slice failure.
Detector misses are part of the routed system; model-only accuracy does not establish the required end-to-end high-risk quality.

feedback.reason: Both models are compared on the same classes and the routed outcome includes the detector-miss path, so the mixed strategy is selected from measured end-to-end behavior rather than incomparable per-class claims.

options.text: Route routine traffic to A and detected high-risk traffic to B; monitor end-to-end quality including misses, allocation, and p95, with uncertainty review.
Use Model B for every request because its 99% high-risk score is the strongest available result.
Use Model A globally because its 0.7-second p95 is safest, and treat the detector as a reporting signal rather than a routing control.
Route detector positives to Model B and declare readiness from Model B's 99% score while excluding detector misses from the quality dashboard.

prompt:
A support classifier receives 40 requests per second. On the same held-out routine and high-risk classes, Model A scores 97% and 93% with 0.7 seconds p95, while Model B scores 98% and 99% with 1.4 seconds p95. A risk detector identifies high-risk traffic with 92% precision and 97% recall.

Which route should be deployed and monitored under these measured constraints?

constraints: The routine task is relatively straightforward.
Production admission requires measured quality as well as latency and cost.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If representative questions exposed complex reasoning that efficient candidates could not handle, a more capable baseline or selective escalation would be justified.
details.errorCorrection: A premium default, model agreement, and a public benchmark do not establish the most efficient model that satisfies this particular task contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends starting with a faster, cost-effective model for many workloads, testing thoroughly, and upgrading only when performance gaps require it.
details.scenarioApplication: Evaluate real product questions, inspect failing slices, and compare measured latency and cost. Use more capable processing only when it addresses a demonstrated gap.
details.transfer: Choose the least expensive and fastest candidate that demonstrates the required task quality, rather than treating price or capability rank as sufficient evidence.

messages.text: This incurs the high-volume premium before establishing need, and model-produced answers are not automatically independent reference labels.
Agreement can include shared errors and doubles routine inference without demonstrating that a second model is necessary.
A general benchmark and advertised timing may not represent the retailer’s questions or production request shape.

feedback.reason: The workload makes efficient inference valuable, but the actual task benchmark must establish quality. Starting with a suitable efficient candidate avoids paying for unproven extra capability on every routine request.

options.text: Start with the most capable model in production, then use its answers as reference labels when measuring cheaper alternatives.
Test an efficient candidate on representative held-out questions and upgrade or escalate only where measured quality requires it.
Use two efficient models and reconcile their labels on every question, treating agreement as the quality gate before comparing cost.
Choose the model with the highest general classification benchmark among candidates whose advertised latency appears compatible.

prompt: A retailer needs to classify 50,000 short product questions per hour under strict latency and cost targets. Representative questions and a held-out quality gate are available. Which initial model-selection approach fits this workload?

constraints: The two request classes have distinct quality and latency requirements.
Routing outcomes and escalation errors can be evaluated.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If routing overhead or misclassification erased the advantage, a simpler shared configuration could be preferable after an end-to-end comparison.
details.errorCorrection: Uniformity, message length, and uncalibrated self-reported confidence do not substitute for the evaluated workload and risk distinction.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes multi-model strategies that use a lower-cost executor for most work and escalate difficult decisions to a stronger advisor or model.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep routine delivery traffic on the evaluated efficient path and use the tested recovery routing and human threshold, measuring misroutes as part of the system quality.
details.transfer: Apply stronger capability where the measured task or consequence requires it, and evaluate the routing decision itself.

messages.text: Uniformity can simplify operations, but it pays the higher cost for routine work without a demonstrated quality need.
Length is not the validated signal for account-recovery difficulty or risk and can misroute short consequential cases.
Self-reported confidence has not been established as a reliable trigger and may miss confidently wrong high-risk recovery answers.
The efficient model has demonstrated that it meets the routine class’s quality requirement.
The difficult class and remaining high-risk cases need the stronger or human capability shown by the evaluations.

feedback.reason: Measured workload differences support different execution paths. Routing should preserve the quality and risk boundaries rather than using one global model or an unvalidated proxy.

options.text: Use the efficient model for the delivery class whose measured quality satisfies its target.
Use the stronger model for both classes so model uniformity becomes the primary operating criterion.
Route requests by character count, using a longer message as the proxy for the measured recovery-risk class.
Send difficult or high-risk recovery cases to validated stronger capability or the required human path.
Run the efficient model first for every case and escalate only when it explicitly reports low confidence in its own answer.

prompt: A support service handles routine delivery questions and difficult account-recovery cases. Benchmarks show that an efficient model meets the delivery target, while a stronger model improves recovery accuracy; some high-risk recovery cases still require a person. Select TWO model-routing choices consistent with these results.
